questions.question: How did the Norman Conquest change the social and political structure of England?
questions.solution_html:
• How did the Norman Conquest change the social and political structure of England?
  • Implementation of Feudal System – introduced by William the Conqueror - centralizing
  • power and reorganizing land ownership - land was granted to Norman lords (barons) in exchange for
  • military service - English peasantry became serfs, bound to the land and under the control of local
  • lords.
  • Redistribution of Land - nearly all Anglo-Saxon nobles lost their lands, which were
  • redistributed to Norman elites - The Domesday Book (1086) was created to document land
  • ownership and resources, strengthening centralized control.
  • Centralization of Power - the monarchy gained significant authority, with William
  • controlling vast swathes of land directly - castles were built across England to assert Norman
  • dominance and suppress rebellion.
  • Changes in Governance - Anglo-Saxon administrative systems, like the shire and hundred
  • courts, were retained but overseen by Norman officials - Norman-French became the language of the
  • ruling class, law, and administration.
  • Transformation of the Aristocracy - Anglo-Saxon nobility was largely replaced by Norman
  • lords, creating a new elite class loyal to William.
  • Cultural and Legal Shifts - Norman customs and laws, such as primogeniture, were introduced.
  • - ecclesiastical reforms aligned the English Church more closely with Rome, replacing Anglo-Saxon
  • clergy with Normans.
  • Military Reorganization - Norman knights and cavalry replaced the Anglo-Saxon fyrd (militia).
  • - castles fortified Norman control and served as military strongholds.
  • Impact on Language and Culture - Norman-French heavily influenced the English language,
  • blending with Anglo-Saxon to form Middle English - architecture, such as Romanesque churches
  • and cathedrals, flourished under Norman influence.
  • Suppression of Rebellion - harsh measures, such as the Harrying of the North (1069–1070),
  • ensured Norman dominance and quashed resistance.
